title: Where to Put Possessives in Norwegian
goal: Place Norwegian possessives before or after nouns with the right meaning and noun form.

objectives.statement: Place Norwegian possessives before or after nouns with the right meaning and noun form.

spans.value: Sara, Jonas, and Emil are packing after a weekend at a cabin. Several bags, jackets, and sets of keys are lying near the door.
Er dette jakka di?
Ja, det er jakka mi. Men hvor er sekken min?

blocks.translation: Yes, that is my jacket. But where is my backpack?

spans.value: Er det sekken din ved døra?

blocks.translation: Is that your backpack by the door?

spans.value: Nei, det er sekken til Jonas. Min sekk er blå.

blocks.translation: No, that is Jonas’s backpack. My backpack is blue.

spans.value: Her er den. Jeg la telefonen din i sekken din.

blocks.translation: Here it is. I put your phone in your backpack.

spans.value: Takk. Og dette er vel nøklene dine?

blocks.translation: Thanks. And these must be your keys?

spans.value: Nei, mine nøkler ligger i lomma mi. De der er nøklene hennes, tror jeg.

blocks.translation: No, my keys are in my pocket. Those are her keys, I think.

spans.value: Everyone is talking about ownership, but the possessives do not always appear in the same place. Sara says both sekken min and min sekk. Jonas says both sekken din and mine nøkler. In the regular common-noun phrases taught in this lesson, the choice changes which part of the message receives attention and pairs with a change in the form of the noun.
A Norwegian possessive (possessiv) can normally come after or before its noun. This lesson practices the regular pattern with common nouns.
In that pattern, when the possessive follows the noun, the noun takes the
definite form
When the possessive comes before the noun in that pattern, the noun takes the
indefinite form
Both phrases identify the same owner. Their usual focus differs.
Possessive after the noun: the neutral pattern
The most common everyday pattern is:
definite noun + possessive
Use this when ownership is ordinary information and no special contrast is needed.

en.value: Your phone is on the table.

spans.value: In the cabin dialogue, Sara first asks:
She is simply looking for it. She does not need to contrast her backpack with anyone else’s yet.
Possessive before the noun: contrast or emphasis
The other pattern is:
possessive + indefinite noun
This order often highlights the owner. It is useful when correcting someone, distinguishing between owners, or making a contrast.

no.value: Dette er min plass, ikke din.

en.value: This is my seat, not yours.

no.value: Våre venner kommer i kveld, men naboens venner kommer i morgen.

en.value: Our friends are coming this evening, but the neighbor’s friends are coming tomorrow.

spans.value: At the cabin, Emil points to the wrong backpack. Sara then says:
Here, min receives extra attention: her backpack, not Jonas’s backpack.

Preposed possessives can also occur for stylistic reasons, especially in more formal language. At this level, the most useful distinction is simple: use the postposed pattern as the everyday neutral choice, and use the preposed pattern when the owner needs contrast or emphasis.

sections.title: The noun form in the regular pattern

spans.value: For the regular common-noun phrases taught in this lesson, moving the possessive is not enough. The noun changes form too.
Each row below lists Neutral placement first, then Emphatic or contrastive placement.
This regular common-noun pattern works with the singular and plural nouns practiced here.

With feminine nouns, this chapter uses forms such as boka mi and mi bok. Bokmål also permits common-gender forms such as boken min and min bok. With either gender pattern, the regular placement pairing taught here remains the same.
Compact rule for the regular common-noun pattern taught here

items.value: After the noun: use the noun’s definite form.
Before the noun: use the noun’s indefinite form.

spans.value: In this taught pattern, the possessive already makes a preposed phrase definite in meaning, so the noun itself does not take the definite ending.

English places possessive determiners such as my, your, and our before the noun. This can lead learners to produce combinations outside the regular Norwegian common-noun pattern taught here, such as an English-like possessive position with a definite noun.
Correct:
Also correct:
In the regular common-noun pattern taught here, the opposite error is leaving the noun indefinite when the possessive follows it.
Correct:
Do not think of one placement as “more possessive” than the other. Both express ownership. The main differences are noun form and information focus.
Compare these two exchanges.
Neutral question
Hvor er brillene dine?
Brillene mine ligger på kjøkkenet.

blocks.translation: My glasses are in the kitchen.

spans.value: Aron is only giving their location. The neutral postposed pattern is natural.
Correction and contrast
Er dette brillene dine?
Nei, mine briller har svarte innfatninger.

blocks.translation: No, my glasses have black frames.

spans.value: Now Aron is distinguishing his glasses from another pair. Placing mine first highlights the owner.
The same contrast appears with other noun types:

en.value: Our cat is sleeping on the sofa.

no.value: Vår katt er inne, men naboens katt er ute.

en.value: Our cat is indoors, but the neighbor’s cat is outside.

no.value: Jeg har lagt passet ditt i skuffen.

en.value: I have put your passport in the drawer.

no.value: Dette er ditt pass; det andre er mitt.

en.value: This is your passport; the other one is mine.

spans.value: The preposed order does not automatically mean that the speaker is angry or speaking loudly. It means that the owner is prominent in the message. Context supplies any stronger emotion.
In the regular common-noun pattern taught here, possessive placement and noun form operate as a pair. When checking one of these phrases, ask two questions:

items.value: Is the possessive before or after the noun?
Does the noun have the form taught for that position?

spans.value: Consider these corrected examples. In each pair, the first sentence can answer a routine ownership question. For the second sentence, imagine that someone has proposed the wrong key owner or compared where two families live:

no.value: Vi besøker foreldrene våre på søndag.

en.value: We are visiting our parents on Sunday.

no.value: Våre foreldre bor i Bergen, men deres foreldre bor i Tromsø.

en.value: Our parents live in Bergen, but their parents live in Tromsø.

spans.value: In the first sentence of each pair, ownership is presented neutrally and the noun is definite. In the supplied correction or comparison context, the second sentence highlights or contrasts owners and follows the taught regular pattern with the noun’s indefinite form.
The group has found most of its belongings, but Emil is still holding a scarf.
Hvem eier dette skjerfet?
Skjerfet mitt er grønt. Det der er ikke mitt.

blocks.translation: My scarf is green. That one is not mine.

spans.value: Mitt skjerf ligger allerede i sekken min.

blocks.translation: My scarf is already in my backpack.

spans.value: Da vet vi fortsatt ikke hvem som eier det.

blocks.translation: Then we still do not know who owns it.

spans.value: Sara begins with the neutral phrase skjerfet mitt while describing her scarf. Jonas chooses mitt skjerf because he is distinguishing his scarf from the unidentified one. In the same sentence, he uses sekken min neutrally because the backpack’s owner does not need contrast.
One sentence can therefore contain both placements. Imagine Emil has mistakenly said that Jonas’s jacket is in the car, and Sara corrects him:

no.value: Min jakke ligger i bilen, men telefonen min ligger her.

en.value: My jacket is in the car, but my phone is here.

spans.value: In this correction context, the first phrase highlights whose jacket is being discussed. The second simply identifies the phone.

The following day, several coworkers are clearing a meeting room. Laptops, notebooks, cups, and chargers have been left on the table. One coworker asks routine questions about where objects belong. Another corrects mistaken assumptions about ownership.

explanation.value: Etterstilt eiendomsord står med bestemt substantiv, mens foranstilt eiendomsord står med ubestemt substantiv.
Et nøytralt svar om plassering bruker «telefonen min». Når eieren framheves, kan vi si «min telefon» med ubestemt substantiv.
Begge plasseringene er grammatiske. Her står det etterstilte eiendomsordet i det nøytrale svaret, og det foranstilte framhever eieren i det andre.

prompt.value: Liv thinks the cup by the window and the chargers on the table belong to her. They both belong to Amir. Build Amir's reply.

explanation.value: Liv tar feil om begge tingene. I rettelsen setter Amir «mine» først for å framheve at laderne er hans, mens «koppen min» bruker det vanlige etterstilte mønsteret om hvor koppen står.

text.value: «Koppen min står vel ved vinduet, og laderne er mine?»

prompt.value: Write a message to a classmate. Explain both places a possessive can go, say when it can go before the noun to show the owner, and give one example of each.

explanation.value: Skill mellom bestemt substantiv med etterstilt eiendomsord og ubestemt substantiv med foranstilt eiendomsord. Den foranstilte formen kan framheve eller kontrastere eieren.
